In [[mathematics]], a '''twisted polynomial'''<ref>{{Cite book |last=Saltman |first=David J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2sIShCIZ_uUC&dq=Twisted+polynomial+ring&pg=PA52 |title=Lectures on Division Algebras |publisher=American Mathematical Soc. |isbn=978-0-8218-8938-1 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gardner |first1=J. W. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=opoxhIF-3moC&dq=Twisted+polynomial+ring&pg=PA115 |title=Radical Theory of Rings |last2=Wiegandt |first2=R. |date=2003-11-19 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-0-203-91335-2 |language=en}}</ref> is a [[polynomial]] over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] of [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] <math>p</math> in the variable <math>\tau</math> representing the [[Frobenius map]] <math>x\mapsto x^p</math>. In contrast to normal polynomials, multiplication of these polynomials is not [[commutative]], but satisfies the commutation rule 
:<math> \tau x=x^p \tau </math>
for all <math>x</math> in the base field.

Over an infinite field, the twisted polynomial ring is isomorphic to the ring of [[additive polynomial]]s, but where multiplication on the latter is given by composition rather than usual multiplication. However, it is often easier to compute in the twisted polynomial ring — this can be applied especially in the theory of [[Drinfeld module]]s.

==Definition==
Let <math>k</math> be a field of characteristic <math>p</math>. The twisted polynomial ring <math>k\{\tau\}</math> is defined as the set of polynomials in the variable <math>\tau</math> and coefficients in <math>k</math>. It is endowed with a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] structure with the usual addition, but with a non-commutative multiplication that can be summarized with the relation <math>\tau x=x^p\tau</math> for <math>x\in k</math>. Repeated application of this relation yields a formula for the multiplication of any two twisted polynomials.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gardner |first1=J. W. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=opoxhIF-3moC&dq=Twisted+polynomial+ring%2C+definition&pg=PA18 |title=Radical Theory of Rings |last2=Wiegandt |first2=R. |date=2003-11-19 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-0-203-91335-2 |language=en}}</ref>

As an example we perform such a multiplication
:<math> (a+b\tau)(c+d\tau)=a(c+d\tau)+b\tau(c+d\tau)=ac+ad\tau+bc^p\tau+bd^p\tau^2</math>

==Properties==
The morphism 
:<math> k\{\tau\}\to k[x],\quad a_0+a_1\tau+\cdots+a_n\tau^n\mapsto a_0x+a_1x^p+\cdots+a_nx^{p^n}</math>
defines a [[ring homomorphism]] sending a twisted polynomial to an additive polynomial. Here, multiplication on the right hand side is given by composition of polynomials.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mora |first=Teo |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8DjzCwAAQBAJ&dq=Twisted+polynomial+ring%2C+Properties&pg=PA257 |title=Solving Polynomial Equation Systems IV: Volume 4, Buchberger Theory and Beyond |date=2016-04-01 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-316-38138-0 |language=en}}</ref> For example 
:<math>(ax+bx^p)\circ (cx+dx^p)=a(cx+dx^p)+b(cx+dx^p)^p=acx+adx^p+bc^px^p+bd^px^{p^2},</math>
using the fact that in characteristic <math>p</math> we have the [[Freshman's dream]] <math>(x+y)^p=x^p+y^p</math>.

The homomorphism is clearly injective, but is surjective if and only if <math>k</math> is infinite. The failure of surjectivity when <math>k</math> is finite is due to the existence of non-zero polynomials which induce the zero function on <math>k</math> (e.g. <math>x^q-x</math> over the finite field with <math>q</math> elements).{{fact|reason=The relations deriving polynomial equality from pointwise equality have not been assumed.|date=March 2015}}

Even though this ring is not commutative, it still possesses (left and right) [[Euclidean division|division algorithms]].
